transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

I feel like I’m constantly trying to make up for what I eat with these intense workouts and routines, and it’s taking over my life. It has gotten to the point where it's draining all my time and energy, and I just don't know how to break the cycle.
When you feel the need to make up for what you eat, do you feel like you have eaten an unusually large amount of food in a short time and lost control over your eating?

Yes, absolutely. After a late shift, I can easily plow through two or three leftover burgers, fries, and half a box of churros in under an hour. Once I start, it's like a switch flips and I completely lose control—even though a part of me wants to stop, my hands just keep reaching for more food.
To help me understand your situation better, could you share your current height and weight, and whether you have recently experienced a significant loss of weight?
I don't have my exact height and weight on hand right now. I haven't really lost any significant amount of weight recently; if anything, I'm just absolutely terrified of gaining weight.
How many times a week do these episodes of overeating and intense workouts typically occur, and how many months has this pattern been going on?

This has been happening at least once a week for the past several months, where I'll binge late at night and then try to undo it with a brutal workout or by forcing myself to throw up. The whole cycle itself has been going on for well over a year now, starting around the time my job announced a big expansion.
You mentioned this happens at least once a week. Do these episodes of overeating and trying to undo them typically occur twice a week or even more frequently?

It definitely happens at least once a week, usually on a night after a late closing shift. Some weeks, if my hours are really irregular or the stress is high, it can definitely happen more than once, maybe twice or even three times. But it's consistently a struggle for me every single week.
Do you set a very specific target weight for yourself that you feel you must stay below, and how much does your body weight or shape influence how you feel about yourself as a person?

I don't have a specific target weight, but if the scale goes up even a single pound or my work polo feels tighter, I completely panic. My weight and shape heavily influence how I see myself, because I'm constantly terrified of looking like the out-of-shape old guy at work instead of the fit, energetic leader I want to be.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a pattern of binge eating (consuming large amounts of food with a loss of control) and inappropriate compensatory behaviors (intense workouts and self-induced vomiting) driven by an intense fear of weight gain and body image concerns. However, the frequency of these episodes is consistently at least once a week (only occasionally twice or three times), which falls short of the strict ICD-10 frequency criterion of at least twice a week for Bulimia Nervosa (F50.2). Additionally, the patient does not set a sharply defined weight threshold. Therefore, the clinical picture is incomplete for F50.2 and is best classified as Atypical Bulimia Nervosa (F50.3).
